# Archaeology of North Korea

## 1. Introduction

The archaeology of North Korea represents the scientific study of human activity in the northern half of the Korean Peninsula from prehistoric times to the present day. This field encompasses the investigation of ancient settlements, burial sites, historical monuments, and cultural artifacts that provide insights into the development of Korean civilization . As one of the most politically isolated nations in the world, North Korea presents unique challenges and opportunities for archaeological research, with limited international access creating both obstacles to academic collaboration and the preservation of sites from modern development pressures .

The Korean Peninsula has a long archaeological history spanning over 600,000 years, from the earliest evidence of human occupation in the Paleolithic period to the sophisticated kingdoms of the medieval era . North Korea's territory contains numerous significant archaeological sites, including the World Heritage-listed Complex of Goguryeo Tombs and Historic Monuments and Sites in Kaesong, which demonstrate the region's importance in East Asian history .

Despite the challenges, North Korean archaeology has produced substantial research 成果，with institutions such as the Institute of Archaeology at the Academy of Social Sciences and the Faculty of History at Kim Il Sung University conducting excavations and publishing academic work . The primary academic journal, "Joseon gogo yeongu" (Joseon Archaeological Research), has been published quarterly since 1986 and contains over 1,600 articles covering various periods of Korean history .

## 2. Historical Development of North Korean Archaeology

### 2.1 Early Period (1945-1960s)

The development of archaeology in North Korea began shortly after the country's establishment in 1945. In 1946, the "Law on the Preservation of Treasures, Relics, and Natural Monuments" was promulgated, establishing a national framework for cultural heritage protection . This was followed by the creation of provincial "Relic Preservation Committees" in 1947 and the Central "North Korean Relic Preservation Committee" .

The first systematic archaeological investigations in North Korea focused on overcoming colonial perspectives and establishing a national historical narrative. Archaeologists concentrated on prehistoric sites and remains related to Gojoseon, the first Korean kingdom, which had been neglected during the Japanese colonial period (1910-1945) . The adoption of Marxist-Leninist methodology influenced research approaches, emphasizing the scientific study of ancient and medieval remains to demonstrate the legitimacy of Korea's historical development .

A significant breakthrough occurred in 1963 with the discovery of Paleolithic lithic artifacts at the Gul Pori site, marking the first known Paleolithic site in Korea . This discovery fundamentally altered understanding of early human occupation on the Korean Peninsula and established the foundation for subsequent Paleolithic research.

### 2.2 Political Transformation (1970s-1990s)

The 1970s marked a critical turning point in North Korean archaeology as the field became increasingly politicized. Unlike South Korea, which experienced rapid academic advancement through large-scale excavations, North Korean archaeology began to demonstrate a markedly political character . This transformation was particularly evident in the interpretation of Bronze Age and Iron Age sites associated with Gojoseon.

In the 1990s, North Korea declared the "Daedong River Culture," which represented a major ideological shift in archaeological interpretation . This concept emphasized the cultural superiority and continuity of the Daedong River region, particularly around Pyongyang, and became a central tenet of North Korean historical narrative. The declaration of this culture created a complete divergence between North and South Korean archaeological interpretations, with the two traditions sharing almost no common perspectives afterward .

The most controversial archaeological event of this period was the 1993-1994 discovery and excavation of the alleged Tomb of Dangun, the mythical founder of Korea who according to legend established Gojoseon in 2333 BCE . In January 1993, Kim Il Sung instructed officials to discover and restore the tomb, stating that it was necessary to "correct the history of Tangun and ancient Korea which had been distorted by the Japanese imperialists" . The excavation reportedly yielded human remains dated to approximately 5,000 years ago, along with Goguryeo-style artifacts . However, the international archaeological community has largely rejected these findings due to methodological concerns and the refusal to share detailed excavation data .

### 2.3 Contemporary Era (2000s-present)

Since the 2000s, North Korean archaeology has continued to develop within its unique political framework while maintaining some degree of international engagement. The publication of "Joseon gogo yeongu" has continued uninterrupted since 1986, with bibliometric analysis revealing the emergence of key researchers such as Seo Guktae (specializing in Neolithic and Bronze Age) and Jang Woojin (specializing in Paleolithic and human evolution) .

International recognition of North Korean archaeological sites has grown with the inscription of three World Heritage Sites: the Complex of Goguryeo Tombs in 2004, Historic Monuments and Sites in Kaesong in 2013, and Mount Kumgang in 2025 . These designations acknowledge the exceptional universal value of these sites while providing a framework for international cooperation in their preservation.

Despite political constraints, there have been limited instances of North-South Korean archaeological cooperation. The most notable example was the joint excavation of the Goryeo palace remains in Kaesong from 2007, conducted in preparation for the World Heritage nomination . This collaboration demonstrated the potential for archaeological cooperation across the Korean divide, though such opportunities remain rare.

## 3. Archaeological Periods and Sites

### 3.1 Paleolithic Period

The Paleolithic period in North Korea extends from approximately 600,000 years ago to around 10,000 years ago, representing the earliest evidence of human occupation on the Korean Peninsula . The most significant early discovery was the Heukyu-ri site in Pyeongyang's Sariwon County, found in 1966, which dates to 600,000-400,000 years ago and represents the earliest known Paleolithic site in Korea .

Major Paleolithic sites in North Korea include:

**Komun Moru Cave** in South Hwanghae Province near Pyongyang is one of the most important Paleolithic sites. Excavated between 1966 and 1970, the cave contains stone implements including hand axes, trapezoidal tools, and edged chisels, along with fossil bones of 29 animal species, 17 of which are extinct . North Korean archaeologists date the site to approximately one million years ago, though international scholars consider the supporting evidence to be limited .

**Chongphadae Cave** in North Hwanghae Province has produced important evidence for human occupation during the late Middle and Late Pleistocene periods. Layers 12 and 13 of the cave contain human fossils, fireplaces, numerous lithic artifacts, and mammal remains, representing new evidence for paleoenvironment and human activities during the late MIS 3 and MIS 2 periods . The site suggests that the central Korean Peninsula may have served as a refugium during glacial periods .

**Ryonggok Cave** near Pyongyang is perhaps the most important Pleistocene hominin fossil site in North Korea . The site contains remains of at least five individuals, with two fairly well-preserved crania (designated #3 and #7) . Analysis suggests these remains represent early modern humans, with the earliest cultural deposits dating to older than 40,000 years ago .

Human fossils discovered in North Korea include the "Ryokpo Man," "Tokchon Man," and "Hwadae Man" from the Middle Paleolithic period, as well as "Seungnisan Man," "Mandal Man," and "Hwangju Man" from the Late Paleolithic . These remains provide evidence for the anthropological succession from early humans to Paleoanthropic and Neanthropic humans in Korea .

### 3.2 Neolithic Period

The Neolithic period in Korea began around 10,000-8,000 BCE and is characterized by the appearance of pottery and microlithic tools . In North Korea, the Neolithic is particularly associated with comb-patterned pottery (Chulmun), which appears around 3000 BCE .

Major Neolithic sites in North Korea include:

**Sop'ohang Shell Mound** is one of the most extensively studied Neolithic sites in North Korea. Located on the west coast, the shell mound contains evidence of early sedentary communities and provides insights into subsistence strategies, including fishing and shellfish gathering .

**Guryongpo Site** in South Hamgyong Province has produced evidence of Neolithic settlement patterns and pottery styles. The site demonstrates the transition from hunter-gatherer to agricultural societies in the region .

The Neolithic period witnessed the development of increasingly sophisticated pottery traditions, with Chulmun pottery characterized by brownish-gray ware decorated with engraved oblique lines . These ceramics are found in lake and shoreline sites, though during the later Neolithic period they also appear inland, suggesting changes in subsistence strategies .

### 3.3 Bronze Age

The Bronze Age in Korea is conventionally dated from around 1500-1000 BCE, though recent archaeological evidence suggests it might have started as early as 2500 BCE . The transition from Neolithic to Bronze Age began around 2300 BCE and continued over 800-900 years .

North Korean Bronze Age archaeology has been significantly influenced by political narratives, particularly regarding the location of Gojoseon, the first Korean kingdom. In the 1960s, Lee Jirin developed the "Liaodong theory" proposing Gojoseon's location in present-day China, but following political pressure, North Korean archaeologists later developed the "Pyongyang theory," which places Gojoseon's capital in Pyongyang .

Important Bronze Age sites include:

**Chongam-ri Earthen Castle** near Pyongyang is a fortification thought to date to the Gojoseon period. The site is similar to other earthen fortifications of the period and provides evidence for early state formation .

**Pyo-dae Site** in the Daedong River basin has revealed important stratigraphic sequences for Bronze Age chronology. The site demonstrates changes in dwelling architecture and pottery styles over time .

The Bronze Age saw the development of complex social structures and the emergence of organized settlements. Mumun pottery culture (1500-300 BCE) is associated with early Gojoseon society, with excavated walled towns and fortifications suggesting organized settlements .

### 3.4 Iron Age and Ancient Kingdoms

The Iron Age in Korea began around 300 BCE and witnessed the development of sophisticated kingdoms, particularly Gojoseon, which is traditionally dated from 2333 BCE to 108 BCE . The kingdom is said to have been founded by Dangun Wanggeom according to Korean mythology, though the historical existence and location of Gojoseon remain subjects of scholarly debate .

#### 3.4.1 Gojoseon

Gojoseon is considered the first kingdom on the Korean Peninsula, though its historical reality and geographical extent are contested . According to Korean tradition, the kingdom was established by the legendary King Dangun in 2333 BCE .

North Korean archaeology has developed a particular interpretation of Gojoseon's history, emphasizing Pyongyang's role as the kingdom's center. The "Pyongyang theory" proposes that Gojoseon's capital Wanggeom-seong was located in present-day Pyongyang, with a secondary capital in the Liaodong Peninsula . This theory was developed to reconcile historical records of Han Dynasty invasions with the political imperative to maintain that Pyongyang was never occupied by China .

#### 3.4.2 Goguryeo

Goguryeo (37 BCE - 668 CE) was one of the Three Kingdoms of Korea and the most powerful kingdom in Northeast Asia during its height. The kingdom's territory included parts of present-day China and Korea, with its capital initially in what is now North Korea before being moved to Pyongyang in 427 CE .

North Korea contains numerous important Goguryeo sites:

**Complex of Goguryeo Tombs** (inscribed as a UNESCO World Heritage Site in 2004) consists of 63 individual tombs from the later Goguryeo kingdom, located in the cities of Pyongyang and Namp'o . The site includes the Tomb of King Tongmyong and the Anak Tomb No. 3, which contains well-preserved murals depicting daily life and mythology .

**Pyongyang City Walls** (National Treasure No. 1 of North Korea) were first constructed during the Goguryeo period and rebuilt during the Goryeo and Joseon periods . The walls represent a combination of plain and mountain fortress styles, with the outer walls spanning 16 km and the inner walls extending 23 km .

**Goguryeo Palace Sites** in Pyongyang have been extensively excavated. From 1991 to 2020, North Korean archaeologists unearthed and identified historical sites and relics dating to the Goguryeo period in the Pyongyang area, confirming that Goguryeo regarded the area as a major regional base from the 1st century .

#### 3.4.3 Balhae

Balhae (698-926 CE) was established by former Goguryeo nobles after Goguryeo's fall to the Silla-Tang alliance. The kingdom is considered by North Korean historiography to be the successor to Goguryeo and an important part of Korean history .

North Korean archaeological sites related to Balhae include:

**Cheonghae Earthen Castle** and **Cheongjin Bugori area ruins** in North Korea are among the 261 Balhae cultural heritage sites identified in the country . These sites demonstrate Balhae's territorial extent and cultural influence in the region.

The study of Balhae in North Korea has become politically significant, with the history of Balhae now an object of active political games related to territorial claims based on alleged archaeological and historical material .

### 3.5 Medieval and Later Periods

#### 3.5.1 Goryeo Dynasty

The Goryeo Dynasty (918-1392) unified the Korean Peninsula under a single government and established its capital in Kaesong (present-day North Korea). The dynasty's archaeological remains in North Korea are particularly well-preserved and significant.

**Historic Monuments and Sites in Kaesong** (inscribed as a UNESCO World Heritage Site in 2013) consists of 12 separate components that together testify to the history and culture of the Goryeo Dynasty from the 10th to 14th centuries . The site includes:

* **Manwoldae Palace** archaeological site - the main palace of the Goryeo Dynasty, completely destroyed during the Red Turban invasions of the 14th century 

* **Kaesong City Walls** - a triple-walled defense system including the Palocham Wall (896 CE), Outer Wall (1009-1029), and Inner Wall (1391-1393)

* **Kaesong Chomsongdae** - an astronomical and meteorological observatory

* **Koryo Songgyungwan** - a former high state education institute that educated Goryeo national officials

* **Royal Tombs** - including the Mausoleum of King Wang Kon (founder of Goryeo) and the Mausoleum of King Gongmin

The site embodies the political, cultural, philosophical, and spiritual values of the Goryeo period, particularly the transition from Buddhism to Neo-Confucianism in East Asia .

#### 3.5.2 Joseon Dynasty

The Joseon Dynasty (1392-1910) established its capital in Seoul but maintained Pyongyang as an important provincial center. Archaeological remains from this period in North Korea include:

**Pyongyang during Joseon** served as the provincial capital of Pyeongan Province . The city's historical monuments include reconstructed gates and walls from the Joseon period, though many were damaged during the Korean War and subsequently rebuilt.

**Military Sites** from the Imjin War (1592-1598) when Japan invaded Korea are scattered throughout North Korea. These include fortress remains and defensive structures that 见证了 the Korean resistance against Japanese invasion.

### 3.6 Modern Period and the Korean War

The Korean War (1950-1953) had a devastating impact on archaeological sites and cultural heritage in North Korea. Many historical buildings and artifacts were destroyed during the conflict .

Archaeological evidence of the Korean War includes:

**Demilitarized Zone (DMZ)** excavations have recovered over 20,000 artifacts, including American body armor, Chinese gas masks, French dog tags, and hundreds of bone fragments . These finds provide insights into the multinational nature of the conflict and the human cost of the war.

**War Damage Sites** such as the Twin Column Tomb, where the DPRK alleged that US forces used the tomb "to lock up and torture our innocent civilians, during which the frescos were ruthlessly destroyed" . Many historical buildings were destroyed during bombings and have been rebuilt, such as the Paeksang Pavilion, which was destroyed during Korean War bombings and rebuilt afterward .

## 4. Archaeological Institutions and Research

### 4.1 Major Institutions

North Korea has established a comprehensive system of archaeological institutions that conduct research, manage cultural heritage, and publish academic work. The two primary organizations are:

**Institute of Archaeology, Academy of Social Sciences** (established in 1954) is the most important archaeological research institution in North Korea . The institute publishes "Joseon gogo yeongu" (Joseon Archaeological Research), which has been published quarterly without interruption since 1986 . The journal contains 1,656 articles between 1986 and 2019, categorized into eight types: research articles, site reports, lectures, data, news, knowledge, political rhetoric, and guidelines .

**Faculty of History, Kim Il Sung University** (founded in 1946) is North Korea's first university and offers degrees in archaeology . The university has approximately 16,000 students and 2,800 faculty members . The Human Evolution and Development History Research Group within the Faculty of History has conducted important research on Paleolithic cave sites .

Other important institutions include:

* **National Bureau for Cultural Property Conservation (NBCPC)** - responsible for implementing the Law on the Protection of Cultural Property (1994) and its Regulations (2009)

* **Korean Cultural Preservation Centre (KCPC)** - authorized by NBCPC to prepare management plans for cultural heritage sites

* **Provincial Cultural Heritage Preservation Committees** - established in each province to manage local archaeological sites and cultural properties 

### 4.2 Academic Publications and Research Output

North Korean archaeological research is primarily disseminated through academic journals and publications. The most important publication is:

**"Joseon gogo yeongu" (Joseon Archaeological Research)** has been published quarterly by the Institute of Archaeology since 1986 and is considered North Korea's preeminent archaeology journal . Analysis of this journal from 1986 to 2019 reveals several key findings:

* Research articles comprise approximately two-thirds of published content (1,062 articles)

* Site reports account for 252 articles

* Key researchers include Seo Guktae (specializing in Neolithic and Bronze Age) and Jang Woojin (specializing in Paleolithic and human evolution), who have each published over 30 research articles

* Kim Incheol is the third most active researcher with 25 research articles and has produced the greatest number of site reports (14)

Other important publications include:

* **"Yoksa kwahak" (Historical Sciences)** - began publication in 1955 and carries interpretative articles, chiefly by To Yuho, director of the Center 

* **"North Korean Periodicals Archaeology Literature Catalogue"** - lists approximately 4,300 academic papers from eight different publications covering archaeology and cultural heritage 

* **"Overview of Korean Archaeology"** - published by the Institute of Archaeology in 1983, providing a comprehensive survey of North Korean archaeological research 

### 4.3 Research Methods and Techniques

North Korean archaeology employs various research methods and techniques, though the degree of international standardization is difficult to assess due to limited access to research facilities and methods.

**Excavation Techniques** are conducted by teams from the Institute of Archaeology and Kim Il Sung University. Major excavations have included:

* The Goguryeo palace sites in Pyongyang (1991-2020) 

* The Goryeo palace remains in Kaesong (joint North-South excavation, 2007)

* Various Paleolithic cave sites, including Chongphadae Cave and Ryonggok Cave 

**Dating Methods** used in North Korean archaeology include:

* Radiocarbon dating - used for organic materials 

* Electron Spin Resonance (ESR) dating - notably used controversially on the Dangun tomb remains 

* Stratigraphic analysis - particularly important for establishing chronological sequences at sites like Pyo-dae

**Conservation and Preservation** efforts are governed by the Law on the Protection of Cultural Property (1994) and its Regulations (2009) . The management plan for the Historic Monuments and Sites in Kaesong, prepared by KCPC and approved by the DPRK government in 2011, includes 5 and 10-year objectives .

### 4.4 International Collaboration and Challenges

International collaboration in North Korean archaeology faces significant challenges due to political isolation, economic sanctions, and restricted access. However, some limited cooperation has occurred:

**North-South Korean Collaboration** has been rare but significant when it occurs. The joint excavation of the Goryeo palace remains in Kaesong (2007) was conducted to prepare for the World Heritage nomination . This collaboration demonstrated the potential for archaeological cooperation despite political tensions.

**China Collaboration** has been more frequent, given geographical proximity and political relations. In the 1960s, a rare joint Chinese-North Korean archaeological excavation took place in China's Liaoning Province at a massive Gojoseon royal necropolis . More recently, Chinese archaeologists have visited North Korea for academic exchanges, such as the 2019 visit by a delegation from the Chinese Academy of Social Sciences .

**UNESCO Engagement** has provided a framework for international recognition and cooperation. North Korea acceded to the World Heritage Convention on July 21, 1998 , and has since had three sites inscribed:

* Complex of Goguryeo Tombs (2004)

* Historic Monuments and Sites in Kaesong (2013) 

* Mount Kumgang (2025)

The World Heritage designation requires 缔约国 to submit regular reports on the state of conservation, providing a mechanism for international monitoring .

**Challenges to International Collaboration** include:

* **Sanctions Impact**: International sanctions have limited North Korea's access to global markets and academic resources 

* **Restricted Access**: Foreign archaeologists face significant barriers to conducting fieldwork in North Korea 

* **Information Sharing**: North Korea has been reluctant to share detailed excavation data and methods, as seen in the Dangun tomb controversy 

* **Political Interference**: Archaeological interpretations are often influenced by political narratives, making objective scientific collaboration difficult 

## 5. Cultural Heritage Protection and World Heritage Sites

### 5.1 Legal Framework

North Korea has established a comprehensive legal framework for cultural heritage protection. The primary legislation is the **Law on the Protection of Cultural Property** (1994), which was amended in 2013 . This law is implemented through the **Regulations on the Implementation of the Law on the Protection of Cultural Property** (2009) .

Key elements of the legal framework include:

* **National Level Protection**: All property components of the World Heritage sites are protected at the national level

* **Buffer Zone Protection**: The mountains and forests in buffer zones are protected by the Law on Environmental Protection (1986) and the Forest Law (1992)

* **Urban Planning Controls**: Urban land within buffer zones is administered under the Land Law (1977) and the Law on City Management (1992)

* **Management Guidelines**: Specific guidelines for protection and management of the Historic Monuments and Sites in Kaesong were prepared and approved in September 2013

### 5.2 World Heritage Sites

North Korea currently has three sites inscribed on the UNESCO World Heritage List:

#### 5.2.1 Complex of Goguryeo Tombs (2004)

The Complex of Goguryeo Tombs was inscribed as North Korea's first World Heritage Site in July 2004 . The site meets UNESCO criteria (i), (ii), (iii), and (iv) and covers 233 hectares with a buffer zone of 1,701 hectares .

**Description**:

The site consists of 63 individual tombs from the later Goguryeo kingdom, located in the cities of Pyongyang and Namp'o . The tombs are particularly renowned for their:

* **Mural Paintings**: Considered masterpieces of the Goguryeo period, the murals provide unique perspectives on daily life, mythology, and court culture 

* **Architectural Ingenuity**: The tombs demonstrate ingenious engineering capabilities, with some featuring sophisticated ceiling designs that require no supports 

* **Historical Significance**: The site provides exceptional testimony to the Goguryeo civilization, which ruled parts of China and Korea from 37 BCE to the 7th century CE 

**Major Components**:

* Tomb of King Tongmyong - the alleged founder of Goguryeo 

* Anak Tomb No. 3 - famous for its well-preserved murals depicting hunting scenes, servants, and astronomical phenomena 

* Twin Column Tomb - notable for its architectural features

* Group of tombs at Jinpha-ri

#### 5.2.2 Historic Monuments and Sites in Kaesong (2013)

The Historic Monuments and Sites in Kaesong were inscribed as a World Heritage Site during the 37th session of the World Heritage Committee in Phnom Penh in June 2013 . The site meets criteria (ii) and (iii) and covers 494.2 hectares with a buffer zone of 5,222.1 hectares .

**Description**:

The site consists of 12 separate components that together testify to the history and culture of the Goryeo Dynasty (918-1392) . The site embodies the political, cultural, philosophical, and spiritual values of the Goryeo period, particularly the transition from Buddhism to Neo-Confucianism in East Asia .

**Key Components**:

* **Manwoldae Palace Site** - the main palace of the Goryeo Dynasty, completely destroyed during the Red Turban invasions 

* **Kaesong City Walls** - a triple-walled defense system including:

 * Palocham Wall (896 CE) - the innermost wall 

 * Outer Wall (1009-1029) - connecting mountains for geomantic protection

 * Inner Wall (1391-1393)

* **Kaesong Chomsongdae** - an astronomical and meteorological observatory

* **Koryo Songgyungwan** - a former national academy that educated Goryeo officials

* **Sungyang Sowon** - a Confucian private school

* **Royal Tombs** - including the Mausoleum of King Wang Kon and the Mausoleum of King Gongmin

#### 5.2.3 Mount Kumgang (2025)

Mount Kumgang (Diamond Mountain from the Sea) was inscribed as North Korea's third World Heritage Site in 2025 . This natural heritage site is known for its scenic beauty and cultural significance.

### 5.3 Challenges in Heritage Protection

North Korean cultural heritage faces numerous challenges in protection and preservation:

**War Damage**: The Korean War caused extensive damage to historical buildings and archaeological sites. Many structures, such as the Paeksang Pavilion, were destroyed during bombings and have been rebuilt . The National Museum of Korea exhibition "6·25 War and the National Museum" displays damaged artifacts including a Joseon military map with North Korean military boot prints and broken ceramics .

**Development Pressure**: As North Korea develops its infrastructure, there is concern that archaeological sites may be damaged or destroyed. The proposed economic cooperation projects between North and South Korea have raised concerns about potential impacts on cultural heritage .

**Lack of International Cooperation**: The isolation of North Korea has limited international assistance for heritage preservation. The country's cultural heritage protection efforts have long been in a closed state, with few cooperative projects with UNESCO, the World Bank, and other international institutions .

**Political Influence on Interpretation**: Archaeological sites are often subject to political narratives that may compromise their historical integrity. The Dangun tomb controversy exemplifies how political considerations can influence archaeological interpretation and public presentation of findings .

**Climate and Environmental Factors**: Natural disasters and environmental degradation pose ongoing threats to archaeological sites. Some sites, such as the petroglyphs at Bangu-dae, require protection from weathering and erosion.

## 6. Notable Archaeological Discoveries

### 6.1 Prehistoric Discoveries

North Korean archaeology has made several significant prehistoric discoveries that have contributed to understanding human evolution and early Korean civilization:

**Paleolithic Discoveries**:

* The **Heukyu-ri site** (1966) in Pyeongyang's Sariwon County is the earliest known Paleolithic site in Korea, dating to 600,000-400,000 years ago 

* **Komun Moru Cave** has produced stone implements and fossil bones dating to approximately one million years ago, though this dating is contested

* **Chongphadae Cave** has revealed human fossils, fireplaces, and lithic artifacts from the late MIS 3 and MIS 2 periods, suggesting the Korean Peninsula served as a refugium during glacial periods 

* **Ryonggok Cave** contains remains of at least five early modern humans, with cultural deposits dating to over 40,000 years ago

**Neolithic Discoveries**:

* **Sop'ohang Shell Mound** provides evidence of early sedentary communities and subsistence strategies 

* Neolithic pottery traditions, particularly comb-patterned (Chulmun) pottery, have been documented across North Korea 

**Bronze Age Discoveries**:

* The transition from Neolithic to Bronze Age began around 2300 BCE and continued over 800-900 years 

* Mumun pottery culture (1500-300 BCE) associated with early Gojoseon society has been identified at sites like Chongam-ri 

### 6.2 Ancient Kingdom Discoveries

**Goguryeo Discoveries**:

* The **Complex of Goguryeo Tombs** includes 63 tombs with exceptional mural paintings that provide unique insights into Goguryeo court life, mythology, and daily activities 

* **Pyongyang City Walls** (National Treasure No. 1) demonstrate the sophisticated fortress architecture of the Goguryeo period 

* Extensive palace excavations in Pyongyang (1991-2020) have confirmed Goguryeo's long-standing occupation of the area 

**Balhae Discoveries**:

* North Korea has identified 261 Balhae cultural heritage sites, including Cheonghae Earthen Castle and Cheongjin Bugori area ruins 

* These sites demonstrate Balhae's territorial extent and cultural connections to Goguryeo

**Goryeo Discoveries**:

* **Manwoldae Palace** in Kaesong, though destroyed in the 14th century, has been extensively excavated and provides insights into Goryeo court architecture and administration 

* The **Royal Tombs of Goryeo** include the mausoleums of King Wang Kon (founder) and King Gongmin, demonstrating the dynasty's sophisticated burial traditions

* **Kaesong City** as a whole represents a well-preserved medieval Korean capital with its triple-walled defense system and administrative buildings

### 6.3 Recent Important Finds

Recent archaeological discoveries in North Korea include:

**Buddhist Artifacts**: In 2025, North Korean archaeologists unearthed a 7-meter-tall Buddha statue at an archaeological site in Yak Jon-ri, South Pyongan Province. The statue was discovered by the Korean Archaeology Institute of the Academy of Social Sciences and the National Authority for the Protection of Cultural Heritage .

**Paleolithic Finds in Southwest North Korea**: In 2019, faculty and researchers from Kim Il Sung University discovered Paleolithic remains including five stone tools, three bone tools, and 732 fossil bones near the Ryesong River .

**Goryeo Era Artifacts**: At Manwoldae Palace, numerous valuable relics from the late Goryeo period have been uncovered, including ceramics, metal items, ancestral tablets, mirrors, and over 3,000 roofing tiles .

## 7. Contemporary Issues and Controversies

### 7.1 Political Influence on Archaeological Interpretation

North Korean archaeology is significantly influenced by political narratives, creating challenges for objective scientific research and international credibility.

**The Dangun Tomb Controversy** represents the most significant example of political interference in North Korean archaeology. In 1993-1994, North Korea claimed to have discovered and excavated the Tomb of Dangun, the mythical founder of Korea who is said to have established Gojoseon in 2333 BCE . The excavation yielded human remains dated to approximately 5,000 years ago using electron spin resonance (ESR) dating . However, this dating method was controversial as ESR is typically used for dating materials over 100,000 years old, not 5,000-year-old remains .

International archaeologists have raised several concerns:

* The refusal to share detailed excavation data and measurement methods 

* The political timing of the discovery, coming shortly before Kim Il Sung's death in 1994 

* The association of the tomb with the "Pyongyang theory" of Gojoseon's location, which serves political objectives 

**The Daedong River Culture Theory** (declared in the 1990s) represents another example of politically motivated archaeological interpretation. This theory emphasizes the cultural superiority and continuity of the Daedong River region around Pyongyang, creating a complete divergence from South Korean archaeological interpretations .

**Balhae Archaeology and Territorial Claims** has become an object of "active political games which are related to territorial claims based on alleged archaeological and historical material" . The interpretation of Balhae history serves both historical and contemporary political purposes.

### 7.2 International Perception and Academic Freedom

North Korean archaeology faces significant challenges in terms of international recognition and academic freedom:

**Academic Freedom Constraints**: The North Korean government severely restricts academic freedom, controlling artistic works and curriculum . The government has restricted academic travel and maintains tight control over all media .

**Information Sharing Issues**: North Korea's reluctance to share detailed excavation data and methods has damaged its credibility in the international archaeological community. The Dangun tomb controversy exemplifies this problem, where North Korea refused to disclose excavation data and measurement methods requested by the archaeological community .

**Bias in Interpretation**: South Korean archaeologists view North Korean archaeological claims with what they term a "dual perspective" - recognizing the importance of North Korean data while questioning its reliability due to political influence .

**Limited International Engagement**: The isolation of North Korea has limited its participation in international archaeological conferences, collaborative research projects, and data sharing initiatives.

### 7.3 Impact of Sanctions and Isolation

International sanctions have had a significant impact on North Korean archaeology:

**Economic Impact**: Sanctions have limited North Korea's access to global markets and academic resources . This has affected the country's ability to purchase modern archaeological equipment, analytical tools, and conservation materials.

**Collaboration Restrictions**: Sanctions have made international academic collaboration difficult, limiting North Korean archaeologists' participation in international conferences, joint research projects, and exchange programs.

**Technology Access**: Restrictions on technology transfer have limited North Korea's ability to adopt modern archaeological techniques and analytical methods.

**Funding Limitations**: The sanctions regime has constrained government funding for archaeological research and site preservation, potentially threatening the long-term conservation of cultural heritage.

### 7.4 Preservation Challenges

North Korean cultural heritage faces multiple preservation challenges:

**War Damage and Reconstruction**: Many historical buildings were destroyed during the Korean War and have been rebuilt, sometimes without complete archaeological documentation of the original structures .

**Development Pressure**: Proposed infrastructure development and economic cooperation projects raise concerns about potential damage to archaeological sites .

**Environmental Threats**: Natural disasters, erosion, and climate change pose ongoing threats to archaeological sites and artifacts.

**Lack of Resources**: Limited funding and technical resources make it difficult to implement modern conservation techniques and protective measures.

**Isolation from International Best Practices**: Limited international engagement means North Korea has been unable to benefit from global advances in archaeological preservation and conservation techniques.

## 8. Conclusion

The archaeology of North Korea represents a unique field of study that combines significant scientific potential with complex political challenges. The country's territory contains numerous sites of exceptional importance for understanding Korean and East Asian history, including three UNESCO World Heritage Sites: the Complex of Goguryeo Tombs, Historic Monuments and Sites in Kaesong, and Mount Kumgang.

The field has made important contributions to understanding human evolution in East Asia, early Korean civilization, and the development of ancient kingdoms like Goguryeo and Goryeo.

However, the discipline faces significant challenges. The politicization of archaeological interpretation, particularly evident in the Dangun tomb controversy and the Daedong River Culture theory, has created tensions between scientific objectivity and political narrative. The isolation of North Korea has limited international collaboration, information sharing, and access to modern archaeological techniques. International sanctions have further constrained resources and cooperation opportunities.

Looking forward, the future of North Korean archaeology will likely depend on several factors:

1. **Political Developments**: Improvements in North-South relations and international engagement could open new opportunities for collaborative research and information sharing.

2. **Technological Access**: Greater access to modern archaeological tools and techniques could enhance the quality and credibility of North Korean research.

3. **Heritage Protection**: Continued efforts to protect and preserve North Korea's rich cultural heritage will be essential, particularly as development pressures increase.

4. **Scientific Standards**: Adherence to international scientific standards and greater transparency in research methods and results will be crucial for building international credibility.

The archaeology of North Korea remains a field of great potential that could significantly advance our understanding of Korean and East Asian history. However, realizing this potential will require a balance between academic freedom, political realities, and international cooperation. As the Korean Peninsula continues to evolve politically, the archaeological record stands as a shared heritage that could one day serve as a bridge for reunification of knowledge and understanding.

The field's challenges also offer important lessons for the broader archaeological community about the intersection of politics and science, the importance of academic freedom, and the universal value of cultural heritage. As international cooperation gradually increases, there is hope that North Korean archaeology will emerge as a fully collaborative and respected discipline within the global archaeological community.

The archaeology of North Korea represents a unique field of study that combines significant scientific potential with complex political challenges.

The country's territory contains numerous sites of exceptional importance for understanding Korean and East Asian history, including three UNESCO World Heritage Sites: the Complex of Goguryeo Tombs, Historic Monuments and Sites in Kaesong, and Mount Kumgang.

North Korean archaeology has produced substantial research 成果, with institutions like the Institute of Archaeology and Kim Il Sung University conducting excavations and publishing academic work through journals like "Joseon gogo yeongu."
The field has made important contributions to understanding human evolution in East Asia, early Korean civilization, and the development of ancient kingdoms like Goguryeo and Goryeo.
However, the discipline faces significant challenges.

The politicization of archaeological interpretation, particularly evident in the Dangun tomb controversy and the Daedong River Culture theory, has created tensions between scientific objectivity and political narrative.
The isolation of North Korea has limited international collaboration, information sharing, and access to modern archaeological techniques.
International sanctions have further constrained resources and cooperation opportunities.
Looking forward, the future of North Korean archaeology will likely depend on several factors.
Improvements in North-South relations and international engagement could open new opportunities for collaborative research and information sharing.
Greater access to modern archaeological tools and techniques could enhance the quality and credibility of North Korean research.
Continued efforts to protect and preserve North Korea's rich cultural heritage will be essential, particularly as development pressures increase.
Adherence to international scientific standards and greater transparency in research methods and results will be crucial for building international credibility.
The archaeology of North Korea remains a field of great potential that could significantly advance our understanding of Korean and East Asian history.
However, realizing this potential will require a balance between academic freedom, political realities, and international cooperation.
As the Korean Peninsula continues to evolve politically, the archaeological record stands as a shared heritage that could one day serve as a bridge for reunification of knowledge and understanding.

The field's challenges also offer important lessons for the broader archaeological community about the intersection of politics and science, the importance of academic freedom, and the universal value of cultural heritage.
As international cooperation gradually increases, there is hope that North Korean archaeology will emerge as a fully collaborative and respected discipline within the global archaeological community.

Mapping North Korean Humanities Research 

Jong-wook HONG 

Why North Korean Humanities? 

This special issue focuses on humanities research in North Korea. When 

many people think of North Korea, the nuclear crisis or the food crisis come 

to mind. North Korea is either demonized as an  axis of evil  that poses a 

threat to humanity, or is presented as a subject of pity in need of 

humanitarian relief. While many people are interested in North Korea, they 

often forget that there are human beings living there, with their own history 

and a love of literature. 

How do North Koreans perceive themselves, what kind of world do 

they live in, and what kind of knowledge have North Korean scholars 

provided to their fellow citizens? In this special issue, we go beyond a review 

of individual studies produced by North Korean humanities researchers to 

examine the characteristics of and changes in North Korean humanities 

itself by mapping the academic community as a whole. In doing so, we hope 

to shed light not only on North Korea, but also on modern academia, 

especially on humanities research on the periphery. Furthermore, we hope 

to lay the groundwork for a better understanding of North Korean society 

and for reconciliation and cooperation with its people.  

> Jong-wook HONG is an associate professor at the Institute of Humanities, Seoul National
> University. E-mail: hongtsky@snu.ac.kr .
> Korea Journal , vol. 63, no. 4 (Winter 2023): 5–15.
> doi: 10.25024/kj.2023.63.4.5

On This Topic 6KOREA JOURNAL / WINTER  2023 

Background to the Special Issue 

There is a large body of research on the humanities in North Korea. I would 

like to introduce here some of the studies that informed the planning of this 

special issue, focusing on research conducted in South Korea. First, there is 

Kang Ho-je’s study outlining the North Korean academic system (Kang 

2007). Although Kang’s focus is on science and technology, that study 

provides important information about the organization and evolution of 

North Korea’s Academy of Sciences. 

In the post-democratic South, the desire to understand North Korean 

society has led to a wave of research on North Korean historiography. These 

studies were undertaken with the aim of overcoming the academic divide by 

introducing the achievements of North Korean historiography to South 

Korean society (Chung et al. 1989; Ahn and Doh 1990). South Korea’s 

National Institute of Korean History (Guksa pyeonchan wiwonhoe) 

analyzed North Korean historiography according to period and theme. This 

led to the systematic organization of North Korean historiography, including 

its institutional aspects (NIKH 2002a, 2003a, 2003b, 2004a, 2004b). More 

recently, a critical analysis based on reflections on nationalism in modern 

historiography has also emerged (D. H. Chung 2001; North Korean 

Historiography Research Group 2003). 

In the field of archaeology, access to North Korean scholarly sources has 

led to the emergence of studies that provide an overview of North Korean 

archaeology (e.g. S. Yi 1992). Since the 2000s, North Korean archaeology has 

been analyzed and evaluated based on newly available archaeological data 

(e.g. K. Yi 2015). Several academic societies have also held conferences on 

North Korean archaeology (e.g. KRAS 2016). Meanwhile, from 2007, the 

National Research Institute of Cultural Heritage (Gungnip munhwajae 

yeonguwon) conducted a joint inter-Korean excavation of the remaining 

Goryeo palaces in Gaeseong (Kaesong), North Korea, to prepare for the 

nomination of the “Historic Monuments and Sites in Kaesong” as a World 

Heritage Site. 

Research on North Korean literature also began in earnest after the 

democratization of South Korean society and the new access to the work of Mapping North Korean Humanities Research 7

North Korean writers. Kim Jae-yong laid the foundation for the study of 

North Korean literature by undertaking a diachronic study of the changes in 

the system and theory of North Korean literature (J. Kim 1994). North 

Korean literary studies have tended to center on changes in party-led literary 

theory and policy, but more recent studies have focused on reconstructing 

various aspects of North Korean literature from a new perspective. 

First, individual books and media contents are being studied to 

reconstruct the production and distribution processes of North Korean 

literature, and to shed light on the country’s cultural infrastructure. In 2018, 

to commemorate the thirtieth anniversary of the release of North Korean 

writers, the Han Sang-eon Cinema Institute organized the exhibition 

“Pyongyang Bookstore,” which brought North Korean literature, music, art, 

theater, and film books, posters, and paintings to the public. The exhibition 

showcased the richness of North Korean culture in the 1950s and 1960s and 

the social foundations of the country’s state-led culture (Han 2018). Kim 

Seong-su provided a comprehensive review of the (North) Korean Writers’ 

Alliance’s organizational magazine,  Joseon munhak  (Korean Literature), 

highlighting the tension between party-led policies and North Korean 

literature (S. Kim 2020). 

Second, the connections between North Korean literature and world 

literature are being highlighted. Park Tae-il and Park Jinyoung reconstructed 

the activities of two representative North Korean translators, Baek Seok and 

Lim Hak-su, respectively, and explored the meaning of world literature in 

North Korean translation theory and socialist education (T. Park 2020; J. 

Park 2015). Zhao Yingqiu and Ko Ja-yeon shed light on aspects and 

meanings of cultural exchanges between North Korea and socialist 

countries, focusing on North Korean writers’ travels to the Soviet Union and 

participation in Asian and African writers’ conferences (Zhao 2021; J. Ko 

2019). 

Itagaki Ryuta recently published a monograph on the life and work of 

North Korean linguist Kim Su-gyeong (Itagaki 2021). Kim was a brilliant 

linguist who studied at Keijō Imperial University and led the standardization 

of the North Korean language. Itagaki’s study of North Korean linguistics 

shows its continuity with colonialism, the influence of North Korean 8KOREA JOURNAL / WINTER  2023 

politics, and its relationship with Soviet linguistics, providing a new 

direction for North Korean humanities research. 

Characteristics of and Changes in North Korean Academia 

Let us now examine the characteristics of and changes in North Korean 

humanities academia over time, with a focus on historical studies, to better 

contextualize the articles comprising this special issue. 

North Korean academia has its origins in the academic system and 

infrastructure created by the Japanese during the colonial period, and with 

the efforts of Koreans to pioneer their own scholarship. However, during the 

colonial period, most higher education institutions were located in Seoul. 

Intellectuals who traveled from Seoul to Pyongyang to build a new socialist 

country following liberation began their studies under difficult conditions. 

Most of them, of course, had studied in Japanese academia. 

Colonial Korea of the 1930s, often referred to as the birth period of 

modern Korean academia, was an incubator for what became North Korean 

humanities. The debate among Marxist historians in 1930s Korea over how 

to view world history’s universality and Asia’s specificity was replayed in 

North Korea in the 1950s. Further, the study of Joseon Korea’s  silhak 

(practical learning) was a key theme of the Joseonhak  (Korean studies) 

movement of colonial Korea, which was led by nationalists and included 

some socialists such as Paik Nam-un. This study of  silhak  later developed in 

earnest in North Korea (Hong 2014). 

The Soviet influence on North Korean academia and culture was 

overwhelming in the early years of the country’s founding. Under the slogan 

“Learn from the Soviet Union,” Soviet studies were actively introduced and 

embraced. The orthodox Marxist-Leninist theories adopted from Soviet 

historiography, along with the  socialist realism  emphasized in Soviet 

literature since the 1930s and the  national history  narrative established in 

Soviet historiography, shaped the direction of North Korean humanities in 

the early years of its founding (Hong 2020). 

By the 1960s, nationalism was on the rise in North Korea. Juche had Mapping North Korean Humanities Research 9

been established as the state ideology, replacing Marxism. History and 

literature also moved away from the orthodox tenets of socialism to 

emphasize the nationalist Juche ideology. State intervention and censorship 

in academia also intensified (Hong 2022). The goal of this special issue is to 

examine how the humanities in North Korea have changed under such 

circumstances. 

Digital Humanities Methodology 

This special issue is the byproduct of a project for the construction of a 

North Korean Humanities Data Archive (NKHDA), conducted by the 

Institute of Humanities at Seoul National University. NKHDA was built over 

a three-year period from 2020 to 2022 with the support of the Seoul 

National University Institute for Peace and Unification Studies. NKHDA 

represents the result of the application of digital humanities methodology to 

North Korean humanities research. 

With the widespread digitization of humanities materials and research 

results in the 21st century, the sharing of humanities knowledge on the web 

is steadily expanding. North Korean humanities research is no exception to 

this trend. NKHDA has adopted semantic data processing, which is a 

qualitative approach to digital humanities. Semantic data processing is a 

methodology suitable for humanities research because it aims to organize 

various layers of information contained in different types of documents into 

a homogeneous format while reproducing the complex semantic 

relationships between them as much as possible (H. Kim et al . 2016). 

NKHDA adopted a wiki as a platform for describing and compiling 

data by multiple people in a web environment. A wiki is a software engine 

that compiles information in a simple markup language, a database that 

organizes and accumulates the compiled information, and a website for 

sharing all of these in a web environment (J. Kim et al. 2021). The widely 

used Wikipedia is a prime example. 

NKHDA was inspired by two digital archives, “Linked Jazz” and 

“Enslaved.” NKHDA’s debt to these two projects is that it centers on “person” 10 KOREA JOURNAL / WINTER  2023 

data, which was implemented as a Knowledge Graph, and takes the 

compilation of Triple (S-P-O) data as the core of its data construction task 

(Heller 2016; Shimizu et al. 2023). 

The application of digital humanities methodologies to the study of 

North Korean humanities is largely due to the vast amount of research and 

information accumulated in the South. The National Institute of Korean 

History has accomplished the feat of archiving North Korean academia itself 

by cataloging historical materials and research output from the North. This 

is an important foundation for building a digital database (NIKH 2001, 

2002b). The National Research Institute of Cultural Heritage has also 

published a list of articles from North Korean archaeological journals such 

as  Joseon gogo yeongu  (Joseon Archaeological Research) (NRICH 2017a, 

2017b). Based on this, a meta-analysis of North Korean archaeology was 

conducted (I. Ko 2018). 

In the aforementioned study on  Joseon munhak  by Kim Seong-su, the 

media analysis table, which summarizes the bibliographical information, 

accounts for more than half of the total. In the future, when the database 

containing information related to  Joseon munhak  is released in the digital 

web environment, it will open a new horizon in the study of North Korean 

literature. 

Introduction to the Articles 

This special issue includes three articles. The article, by Ryu Intae and Hong 

Jong-wook, is a full report on the project for constructing the North Korean 

Humanities Data Archive. This article first summarizes the theoretical and 

technical background of NKHDA. It is a systematic and comprehensive 

explanation of the aforementioned characteristics of and changes in North 

Korean academia and digital humanities methodology. This article also 

describes the process of building the NKHDA and introduces the trials and 

errors in that process. In designing the ontology and creating the triple data, 

efforts were made to capture the characteristics of the North Korean 

humanities, which are historically connected to colonial Korea and Mapping North Korean Humanities Research 11 

contemporaneously connected to Soviet academia. At the same time, the 

process did not lose sight of the state-driven nature of the humanities in 

North Korea, something that becomes evident in the process of archiving 

the materials and tracing the development of debates. The article by Ryu and 

Hong also introduces how NKHDA, which combines network knowledge 

graphs and wiki pages, can function as an educational platform for North 

Korean humanities and digital humanities in university classrooms. 

The following article, by Ko Ilhong, analyzes the academic journal 

Joseon Archaeological Research  (Joseon gogo yeongu ) using digital humanities 

methodology to reveal the characteristics of the North Korean archaeological 

community and its changes over time. Ko visualizes the results of bibliometric 

analysis using semantic networks along with word clouds to demonstrate 

the efficiency of digital humanities approaches for large data sets. In this 

study, the bibliographic data of  Joseon gogo yeongu , rather than its contents, 

have been selected as the subject of analysis. This methodological approach 

was influenced by the philosophy and goals of  distant reading , a concept that 

originally emerged in the context of literary criticism but has since been 

used in the production of intellectual histories in a wide range of disciplines 

(Underwood 2016). In so doing, Ko reveals the existence of certain 

archaeologists whose importance has been overlooked in the discourse on 

North Korean archaeology in the South. 

Next, Kim Heon’s article is a comparative analysis of the prefaces of 

three translations of  The Iliad  by Lim Hak-Su composed at different times. 

Lim Hak-Su, who studied in the English Department of Keijō Imperial 

University in Japanese colonial Korea, first published his translation of  The 

Iliad  in 1940–1941, at the height of the Second Sino-Japanese War. The 

book’s preface begins with a rave review of  The Iliad  and maintains an 

emotional and romantic tone throughout. Lim Hak-Su, who participated in 

the founding of North Korea and went on to become a professor at Kim Il 

Sung University, published a second translation in 1963. In his preface to 

this edition, Lim defined Homer’s  Iliad  as a “people’s epic” and referenced 

Marx and Engels to support his assessment of  The Iliad . In the preface to his 

third translation, published in 1989, the perspectives of Marx and Engels are 

removed and the teachings of Kim Il-sung are introduced. While Kim 12 KOREA JOURNAL / WINTER  2023 

Heon’s study does not directly apply a digital humanities methodology, it 

does share a research question with other members of the North Korean 

humanities research team in that it focuses on historical continuity with the 

colonial period and the contemporary influence of socialist knowledge 

centered on the Soviet Union. 

One more paper was prepared for this special issue. Jang Moon-seok 

and Choi Kyung-hee proposed to understand North Korea’s publication of 

the  World Literature Anthology  (Segye munhak seonjip ) as a state-led 

monumental cultural project. Their paper argues that the publication of the 

World Literature Anthology  was a self-making project in which North Korea 

invented a literary language all while educating the sensibilities of the 

country’s emerging reading public. This paper by Jang and Choi is  comple -

mentary  to Kim’s in that Lim’s translation of  The Iliad  appeared in the first 

volume of that  World Literature Anthology . Due to the authors’ circumstances, 

this paper regrettably could not be published as part of the current special 

issue, but it is expected to be published soon in a future issue of the  Korea 

Journal . Readers are encouraged to refer to this paper as well. Mapping North Korean Humanities Research 13

*   [![Image 20: Well with stone masonry](https://kfausa.org/wp-content/uploads/2021/07/6-14.jpg)](https://kfausa.org/wp-content/uploads/2021/07/6-14.jpg)
*   [![Image 21: Bottom of a well with sediment and a wooden frame lining](https://kfausa.org/wp-content/uploads/2021/07/7-12.jpg)](https://kfausa.org/wp-content/uploads/2021/07/7-12.jpg)
*   [![Image 22: A light-brown wooden comb with the handle at the top and teeth extending down from it, resting on a white surface next to a ruler marked in centimeters](https://kfausa.org/wp-content/uploads/2021/07/8-9.jpg)](https://kfausa.org/wp-content/uploads/2021/07/8-9.jpg)
*   [![Image 23: Four pottery fragments from an archeological site are shown in an eye-level shot](https://kfausa.org/wp-content/uploads/2021/07/9-9.jpg)](https://kfausa.org/wp-content/uploads/2021/07/9-9.jpg)
*   [![Image 24: Three rusty, metal pieces on a white background with a ruler below to show the scale](https://kfausa.org/wp-content/uploads/2021/07/10-13.jpg)](https://kfausa.org/wp-content/uploads/2021/07/10-13.jpg)
*   [![Image 25: Stone Go board fragment excavated from Goguuryeo Well No. 1 in Rimheung-dong is laid on a white surface next to a scale](https://kfausa.org/wp-content/uploads/2021/07/11-10.jpg)](https://kfausa.org/wp-content/uploads/2021/07/11-10.jpg)
*   [![Image 26: Stone Go board fragments discovered at Imheunghyeon-dong Goguryeo Well No. 1 are restored](https://kfausa.org/wp-content/uploads/2021/07/12-12.jpg)](https://kfausa.org/wp-content/uploads/2021/07/12-12.jpg)
*   [![Image 27: Wooden object from an archaeological dig](https://kfausa.org/wp-content/uploads/2021/07/13-10.jpg)](https://kfausa.org/wp-content/uploads/2021/07/13-10.jpg)

Researchers of the Faculty of History of Kim Il Sung University have recently made comprehensive studies of historical sites and relics unearthed up to now in the Rimhung-dong area, Taesong District, Pyongyang, and made public the result which is of great significance in clarifying the history of Koguryo.

From Juche 80 (1991) to Juche 109 (2020) they unearthed and ascertained the historical sites and relics dating back to the period of Koguryo in the above-said area and, in the course of this, made clear afresh that Koguryo, from the outset of the first century, regarded the area as a major regional base and transferred its capital to the walled city of Pyongyang and developed culture.

In the area they discovered some building sites, two wells (Nos. 1 and 2), one underground structure built with bricks, many pieces of roofing tiles and earthenware, etc.

The wells are located about 2 500 metres south of the seat of Rimhung-dong, Taesong District. At the time of discovery, their inner facilities remained intact but some upper parts of their walls were broken.

The first well was made by hardening the bottom with small gravels, sand and clay, installing a square wooden frame with a side of 98cm and a height of 56cm, and piling up the walls with dressed stones of a quadrangular-pyramid type into an octagonal shape and then into a round plane.

Unearthed in the well were pieces of stone _paduk_(go) board, roofing tiles, earthenware, iron pot, lacquered wooden jar, etc.

The second well was made by hardening the bottom by the same method as was used to make the first well, installing a square wooden frame with a diameter of 100cm, and piling up the walls with river gravels up to 160cm and then with flat stones.

Unearthed there were many pieces of earthenware, clay _paduk_(go) board, bamboo comb, etc.

Also discovered in the above-said area were a building site with four cornerstones, two underground drains filled with river stones and an underground brick structure with a width of 150-160cm from south to north, a length of 200cm from east to west and a height of about 90cm. A large number of relics of various kinds were collected around the area.

Through the discovery, the researchers verified a new aspect of the developed culture in Koguryo.

They proved that the pieces of stone _paduk_ board discovered for the first time in the first well were a board with 19 grids belonging to the earliest one in the world, and that the _paduk_ board of Koguryo had been handed down via Koryo to the end of the feudal Joson dynasty.

They also made clear that underground water was filtered again in the wells and wooden frames were used as they were good for the cleaning, and thus identified Koguryo’s technology of improving water quality in the wells.

The Archaeology Society of the DPRK acknowledged the great academic significance of those historical sites and relics, and the Non-Permanent Tangible Heritage Examination and Appraisal Committee assessed their values and registered the two wells on the list of preserved sites.

# Radiocarbon Dates Documenting the Neolithic-Bronze Age Transition in Korea 

## Item Type Proceedings; text 

## Authors Kim, J. C.; Bae, C. J. 

## Citation Kim, J. C., & Bae, C. J. (2010). Radiocarbon dates documenting the Neolithic-Bronze Age transition in Korea. Radiocarbon, 52(2), 483-492. 

## DOI 10.1017/S0033822200045513 

## Publisher Department of Geosciences, The University of Arizona 

## Journal Radiocarbon 

## Rights Copyright © by the Arizona Board of Regents on behalf of the University of Arizona. All rights reserved. 

## Download date 21/12/2025 15:06:26 

## Item License http://rightsstatements.org/vocab/InC/1.0/ 

## Version Final published version 

## Link to Item http://hdl.handle.net/10150/654300 © 2010 by the Arizona Board of Regents on behalf of the University of Arizona  

> Proceedings of the 20th International Radiocarbon Conference, edited by A J T Jull RADIOCARBON, Vol 52, Nr 2–3, 2010, p 483–492

483 

RADIOCARBON DATES DOCUMENTING THE NEOLITHIC-BRONZE AGE TRANSITION IN KOREA 

Jong Chan Kim School of Physics, Seoul National University, Seoul 151-742, Korea. Email: jckim@phya.snu.ac.kr. Christopher J Bae Department of Anthropology, University of Hawai’i, 2424 Maile Way, Saunders Hall 346, Honolulu, Hawaii 96822, USA. Corresponding author. Email: cjbae@hawaii.edu.  

> ABSTRACT. We report radiocarbon dates for ~150 archaeological sites in Korea belonging to the Neolithic-Bronze Age transition period. From the present compilation, we find that the Neolithic-Bronze Age transition in Korea started as early as ~2300 BC and continued over the course of 800–900 yr with peaks representing population increases occurring 2–3 times. Compared with cases in other regions of the world, the Neolithic-Bronze Age transition in Korea was similar in both magni-tude and transition time. However, the process in Korea appears to have occurred about 2000 yr later. Further, we find that the attempt to explain the Neolithic-Bronze Age transition in Korea as a migration hypothesis based only on a sudden population increase is not tenable.

INTRODUCTION 

One of the most debated topics in Korean archaeology is the nature of the Neolithic-Bronze Age transition, a transition that is primarily from a hunting-gathering-fishing lifestyle to reliance on full-scale plant and animal domesticates (W Y Kim 1986; Heu 1991; Nelson 1992, 1993; Rhee and Choi 1992; Norton 2000, 2007; Lee 2001; J S Kim 2002a,b). In particular, there are 2 main arguments currently being debated: 1) the transition is due primarily to an influx of farmers migrating from the north; and 2) the transition is due to increasing indigenous population growth (see above refer-ences). Unfortunately, these interpretations have often relied on a limited number of excavations and a paucity of 14 C dates from the time period in question (about 2800–4900 BP). The intent of our paper is to present an updated compilation of 14 C dates from sites in Korea that date to the Late Neolithic and Early Bronze Age. These data are primarily derived from the Seoul National Univer-sity Accelerator Mass Spectrometry (SNU-AMS) laboratory (Kim et al. 2006a,b) and culled from published literature (Nelson 1993) when applicable. Thus, we present a comprehensive range of 14 Cdata currently available in Korea for this time period. In Korea, the Neolithic is sometimes referred to as the Chulmun period, and the Bronze Age is sometimes referred to as the Mumun period (sim-ilar to the Japanese Jomon and Yayoi). Chulmun means having comb decorations and Mumun means no decoration on the pottery surface. Thus, the presence/absence of pottery decoration is the primary way of discerning whether a Korean site belongs to the Neolithic or the Bronze Age (for reviews see W Y Kim 1986; Nelson 1993; Norton 2000; Choe and Bale 2002; J S Kim 2002b). 

MATERIALS AND METHODS 

The 14 C dates reported here are derived primarily from charcoal samples. Marine samples such as shells from middens are excluded since the marine calibration has not been well established in Korea. However, charcoal samples from shell middens were included. A total of 148 14 C dates are presented in Table 1, with each 14 C date representing a particular settlement (see Figure 1 for loca-tions). The number of settlements coincides only approximately with the number of excavation sites, since in some cases, 1 site produced 2 or more settlements of different occupation periods. If there are 2 clusters of 14 C dates in a certain site, we regard them as 2 settlements, thus, 2 represen-484 J C Kim & C J Bae 

tative dates. Here, we designate a set of 14 C dates as a cluster when they are distributed continuously without any significant interruption. Figure 1 Approximate locations of settlements studied in this work. Numerical IDs taken from the first column of Table 1. Neolithic-Bronze Age Transition in Korea 485 The particular dates chosen for a particular settlement were the oldest 14 C date in the case of Early Bronze Age settlement, and the youngest 14 C in the case of Late Neolithic settlement. The rationale for this selection was because we were interested in evaluating the variation between the upper bound of the Bronze Age and the lower boundary of the Neolithic in Korea. Example 2: Siheung Neunggok-dong Site (Figure 3) 

Two settlements are separated by a ~1500-yr hiatus. We take 2 representative dates from these 2 set-tlements, 3000 BP for the Early Bronze Age and 4500 BP for the Late Neolithic. 

Example 3: Sinmaeri Site (Figure 4) 

Two Late Neolithic settlements with 14 C dates of 4100 and 4800 BP, respectively. These 2 settle-ments are well separated with a ~700-yr hiatus in between. The Bronze Age date of 2700 BP is not used since it is beyond the scope of the present study. 

Example 4: Janggeum-dong Shellmound (Figure 5) 

This Bronze Age site is located in Incheon, a Yellow Sea coastal city due west of Seoul. The site is a shellmound and samples used for dating were charcoal fragments excavated from the shellmound. The date 3600 BP was chosen as representative for this settlement and is one of the earliest Bronze Age dates. > Example 5: Cheoljeong Site (Figure 6)

The earliest Bronze Age site is reported from the inland Kangwon Province area. We interpret this site as a continuous Bronze Age settlement beginning at 3800 BP and lasting up to 1900 BP. The date 3800 BP could have been anomalous, but since the 2 14 C dates are concordant, we interpret this age to be representative for this Bronze Age settlement. The date 3800 BP marks the upper boundary of the incipient Bronze Age together with the date of 3600 BP of Janggeum-dong mentioned above. 

> RESULTS AND DISCUSSION

Figure 7 shows the distribution histogram of representative dates for the 148 settlements. In this his-togram, all BP values were truncated in units of 100 yr. Three different bars represent the Neolithic, Bronze Age, and Neolithic-Bronze Age, respectively, with each bar shaded differently. Settlements not clearly identifiable as either Neolithic or Bronze Age were denoted as “Neolithic-Bronze Age,” and the 14 C dates for these settlements were usually regarded as outliers. As evidenced in Figure 6, although the Bronze Age is clearly observed by ~3000 BP, the inception of the Bronze Age may have started as early as about 3800–3900 BP. This early age for the beginning of the Bronze Age in Korea would make the Korean case contemporary to those of the Longshan and Erlitou Bronze Age cultures in China (Lu and Yan 2005; Shao 2005). Figure 4 14 C dates distribution of the Sinmaeri site Figure 5 14 C dates distribution of the Janggeun-dong shellmound 490 J C Kim & C J Bae 

Further support for an earlier Neolithic-Bronze Age transition in Korea can be found in archaeolog-ical sites in the Tumen River basin (North Korea) and neighboring regions. For example, Incipient Bronze Age settlements have been identified in the Yanbian area in Jilin Province in China and the Southern Primorye region of Russia, which have been dated to about 4000 and 3500 BP (Kang 2007). This is comparable to the dates for the Korean Neolithic-Bronze Age transition period observed in the present study. The solid line in Figure 7 is a smoothed curve denoting the total number of settlements as a function of years BP and could be interpreted in terms of trends in population growth and decline. It is inter-esting to note that there are 2 major increases in this curve during the Neolithic-Bronze Age transi-tion. The first one, a slight increment, occurs at ~4500 BP. The second increase begins at ~3700 BP and triples by 3000 BP. The second one is due to the gradual growth of the Incipient Bronze Age cul-Figure 6 14 C dates distribution of the Cheoljeong site Figure 7 Distribution histogram of representative dates for the 148 settlements Neolithic-Bronze Age Transition in Korea 491 ture, which began around 3800~3900 BP, and is therefore associated with the Neolithic-Bronze Age transition in Korea. In some 14 C-based demographic studies, the number of settlements was weighted by settlement duration. For example, Fiedel and Kuzmin (2007) segmented each settlement into 1000- 14 C yr inter-vals and the number of occupancy (number of centroids) is weighted accordingly. Settlements in the Neolithic-Bronze Age transition in the Korean Peninsula have a duration ranging from about 100 to 1000 yr. These duration times are just in the range of the old-wood effect. Therefore, it could be dis-putable to associate the measured 14 C date spreads with the actual duration time of the settlement. Furthermore, duration times for most of sites in the present study have not been determined yet. For this reason, the duration time has not been taken into account in our analysis above. 

CONCLUSIONS 

From the present compilation, we find that the Neolithic-Bronze Age transition in the Korean Pen-insula began as early as ~2300 BC and continued over the course of 800–900 yr with peaks repre-senting population increases occurring 2–3 times. Compared with cases of transition to farming in other regions of the world (Hanson 2000), the Neolithic-Bronze Age transition in Korea was similar in both magnitude and transition duration. However, the Korean transition occurred about 2000 yr later. Thus, we find that the attempt to explain the Neolithic-Bronze Age transition as a migration hypothesis based only on a sudden population increase in Korea is not tenable. 

ACKNOWLEDGMENTS 

We wish to express thanks to the staff and crew of the Seoul National University AMS facility for their untiring efforts and perseverance. Without their help, this work would not have been possible. We thank Sarah Nelson for many constructive comments on an earlier draft of this manuscript. We take full responsibility for any errors that may be present.

# Sedentism, Territorial Circumscription, and the Increased Use of Plant Domesticates Across Neolithic- Bronze Age Korea 

CHRISTOPHER ]. NORTON IT IS CLEAR THAT THE ORIGINS AND SPREAD OF AGRICULTURE from several core regions around the world had a pronounced effect on our planet, and this phe-nomenon is considered to be one of the most fundamental economic changes in our collective human history. Why this economic transition occurred is still a subject of great debate. Comprehensive edited texts covering this subject and published just in the last decade or SQ alone include the following: Cowan and Watson 1992; Gebauer and Price 1992; Harris 1996; Price and Gebauer 1995 (see Smith 1998, 2001 for a recent comprehensive review of the subject). Never-theless, few of these edited volumes include studies from East Asia and more spe-cifically Korea. This essay adds the Korean Holocene record to the discussion that attempts to address the processual "why" plant domesticates spread across Eurasia. 1

In East Asia, ample archaeological evidence exists that suggests that the origins of millet and rice agriculture occurred in two separate locations. Evidence of fox-tail millet (Setaria italica) agriculture first appears in the archaeological record in northern China between 9000 and 8000 years B.P. at Cishan and Cha-hai. North-east Asia, with a cool and dry climate, was and is much better suited for millet cultivation. Rice (Oryza sativa) production appears slightly later in southern-central China at the site of Hemudu near Lake Taiku in the Lower Yangzi Valley between 7000 and 5900 years B.P. Southeast and South Asia, with its hot and hu-mid climate, was and is an ideal region for rice to grow. In fact, wild rice (0. ruji-pagan) has been known to grow in monsoon Asia from the Himalayas to the Malay Peninsula and even as far north as the Yangzi River (S. M. An 1991, 2004; K. C. Chang 1986; T. T. Chang 1976, 1983; Crawford 1992; Crawford and Chen 1998; Glover and Higham 1996; Heu 1991; Higham 1995; Higham and Lu 1998; Ho 1977; Smith 1998; Zhao 1998). It is currently accepted that Korea was a secondary region for agricultural ori-gins. That is, rice and millet domestication originated in China and later spread across the Korean Peninsula (S. M.
